title: Let the Barbarians In: How AI Can Accelerate Systems Performance Research

mechanism.domainTask: Empirical evaluation of AI-driven research frameworks on systems-performance optimization tasks
mechanism.populationDetail: Table 1 states all three evaluated ADRS frameworks use island-based populations, although each uses different within-island archives and search procedures.
mechanism.archiveDetail: OpenEvolve archive internals are not specified; GEPA uses per-instance Pareto frontiers and ShinkaEvolve weighted Pareto archives. MAP-Elites is attributed to AlphaEvolve, not the evaluated frameworks collectively.
mechanism.replacementDetail: This empirical report compares existing framework configurations and does not define one aggregate survivor/replacement protocol.
mechanism.generationDetail: The paper describes generic solution generation/refinement and compares frameworks with different operators, but does not specify a single shared parent-offspring relation across its case studies.
mechanism.feedbackDetail: Structured and qualitative feedback are analyzed across heterogeneous systems; exact fields and reuse differ by case study and framework.
mechanism.parentSelectionDetail: OpenEvolve samples one parent per island with exploration/archive/random modes; GEPA samples from per-instance Pareto frontiers; ShinkaEvolve weights Pareto-archive sampling by score, novelty, and children. These belong to the evaluated systems, not a new selector proposed by this report.
mechanism.outOfTaxonomy: The paper is a cross-framework empirical systems-research study and design-guidance report, rather than a single evolutionary method; mechanism fields are heterogeneous and framework-attributed.

provenance.sourcePdf: papers/Let the Barbarians In How AI Can Accelerate Systems Performance Research.pdf
provenance.citationWarning: Canonical key barbariansgate refers to the earlier title/eprint, while this extended v4 PDF is titled Let the Barbarians In. Do not attribute AlphaEvolve MAP-Elites to OpenEvolve or the report. Existing parent-selection citation is comparative; evaluator context and parent-selection rule are distinct.
